findings.paper_title: 26 OxCity LG Reserve Risk Assessment Report - Final
findings.headline: EY links the timing of the historic assurance rebuild to upcoming Local Government Reorganisation
findings.detail: EY says that avoiding further delay in rebuilding assurance over the Council's historic position is essential, and that the timing is critical because of upcoming Local Government Reorganisation.
findings.matters: Reorganisation timing affects how and when historic reserve balances are assured, which matters to any council or lender working through a reorganisation.
findings.figures: None stated
findings.quote: which is critical given the timing of upcoming Local Government Reorganisation

findings.paper_title: 26 OxCity LG Reserve Risk Assessment Report - Final
findings.headline: EY will seek a variation to its scale fee for the reserves risk assessment and the historical assurance rebuild
findings.detail: EY says the risk assessment, the preparation of the MHCLG submission and the drafting of the addendum are outside the scale fee. Procedures to rebuild historical assurance will also fall outside it, and EY will report the agreed costs later.
findings.matters: Additional audit fees for historic rebuild work are a cost a finance director must budget for, and the amount is not yet known.
findings.figures: None stated; the cost has not yet been agreed
findings.quote: we will seek a variation to the scale fee to reflect these changes to the scope of our work

findings.paper_title: 26 OxCity LG Reserve Risk Assessment Report - Final
findings.headline: EY says the Council's progress 'falls behind' the expected LARRIG 01 timescales for rebuilding audit assurance
findings.detail: The paper compares the Council's progress with the illustrative timeline in the NAO's LARRIG 01 guidance and concludes that it is behind. EY states that the natural rebuild must start before the historic gaps can be addressed.
findings.matters: A council that is behind the national reset timeline is a useful reference point for other councils assessing where they stand against the same guidance.
findings.figures: Expected assurance timeline reference: 2023/24, 2025/26, 2026/27
findings.quote: In our view, the Council's progress falls behind the expected timescales set out in LARRIG 01.

findings.paper_title: 26 OxCity LG Reserve Risk Assessment Report - Final
findings.headline: Assurance could not be obtained over elements of the Capital Financing Requirement in the 2024/25 audit
findings.detail: The paper says the shortfall relates to capital debtors and capital leases. EY links this to the Capital Adjustment Account and the Capital Receipts Reserve, both of which are rated Significant Risk.
findings.matters: The Capital Financing Requirement drives borrowing headroom, so unverified elements matter to lenders and to finance directors assessing capital financing capacity.
findings.figures: None stated
findings.quote: assurance could not be obtained over certain elements of the Capital Financing Requirement due to insufficient supporting evidence for capital debtors and capital leases.

findings.paper_title: 26 OxCity LG Reserve Risk Assessment Report - Final
findings.headline: A 2024/25 prior-year adjustment restated the Capital Grants Unapplied Account by £16.8 million, relating to grant income timing
findings.detail: EY reports that the adjustment arose from the timing of grant income recognition. Combined with the significant weakness reported, this leads EY to rate the Capital Grants Unapplied Account as a Significant Risk.
findings.matters: A restatement of this size in grant accounting is a concrete example of the misstatement risk that other councils with grant-funded capital programmes should consider.
findings.figures: £16.8 million restatement
findings.quote: a prior-year adjustment identified during the 2024/25 audit resulted in a £16.8 million restatement associated with the timing of grant income recognition.

findings.paper_title: 26 OxCity LG Reserve Risk Assessment Report - Final
findings.headline: EY rates the General Fund balance, the Housing Revenue Account and the Capital Receipts Reserve as 'Significant Risk'
findings.detail: The paper assigns the 'Significant Risk' rating to seven reserves, including the General Fund balance, the Housing Revenue Account, the Capital Receipts Reserve, the Capital Grants Unapplied Account, the Revaluation Reserve, the Capital Adjustment Account and the Deferred Capital Receipts Reserve. Four reserves are rated 'Higher inherent risk'.
findings.matters: A finance director comparing reserve audit risk across councils can use this rating split as a benchmark, and a lender can see which usable reserves carry the highest assurance uncertainty.
findings.figures: 7 reserves rated 'Significant Risk'; 4 reserves rated 'Higher inherent risk' (counted from the paper's dashboard). Opening balance for the Housing Revenue Account was last fully audited for 20/21.
findings.quote: Accordingly, the reserve has been assessed as a Significant Risk.

findings.paper_title: 26 OxCity LG Reserve Risk Assessment Report - Final
findings.headline: EY says pre-2023/24 assurance gaps, particularly on reserves, cannot be sufficiently addressed within the 2025/26 audit
findings.detail: EY gives four reasons: the scale and complexity of historic balances, insufficient historic evidence, limited management capacity, and unresolved control deficiencies from prior years. It will reperform the risk assessment during 2026/27 audit planning.
findings.matters: This tells other councils, and lenders relying on audited reserves, that the historic rebuild may not be completed through the normal annual audit cycle.
findings.figures: None stated
findings.quote: cannot be sufficiently addressed as part of the 2025/26 audit to support future progression towards qualified or unmodified audit opinions

findings.paper_title: 26 OxCity LG Reserve Risk Assessment Report - Final
findings.headline: The 2023/24 and 2024/25 audits of Oxford City Council each ended in a disclaimer of opinion, issued because of the backstop
findings.detail: EY states that the auditor could not form an opinion on the financial statements in either year. The paper frames the rebuild of assurance as a multi-year process that depends on the Council's 2025/26 financial statements and working papers.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council, or a lender, needs to know how long a disclaimer-driven assurance gap takes to close and what the Council's opening reserve balances are now exposed to.
findings.figures: Disclaimers of opinion for 2023/24 and 2024/25
findings.quote: In 2023/24 and 2024/25 a disclaimer of opinion was issued due to the application of the backstop.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 Service Risk Register - Risks only
findings.headline: Housing workforce risk, scored 12 (probability 3, impact 4), records that 'Interim staff are more expensive than permanent staff and can leave at short notice'.
findings.detail: The register links reliance on interim workforce to instability and loss of skills and knowledge in the HRA. It also notes significant competition in the market for skilled new staff. The risk is owned by Nerys Parry.
findings.matters: A housing service leaning on interim staff to hold its HRA together is an added cost and continuity risk that finance and HR teams at other councils will recognise.
findings.figures: risk score 12 (probability 3, impact 4)
findings.quote: Interim staff are more expensive than permanent staff and can leave at short notice.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 Service Risk Register - Risks only
findings.headline: Waste risk, scored 12 (probability 3, impact 4), links ODS commercial waste net income to 'dividend payments to the Council which underpin other service delivery'.
findings.detail: The risk covers higher costs and complexity from changes to statutory obligations and to funding for domestic waste services, as well as competition in commercial waste. The register says domestic collection is a statutory requirement. The risk is owned by Carolyn Ploszynski.
findings.matters: It names a dividend from a council-owned company as a source of funding for other services, which a finance director elsewhere with a similar arrangement will want to check.
findings.figures: risk score 12 (probability 3, impact 4)
findings.quote: If the net income ODS derives from commercial waste operations reduces this could also impact on dividend payments to the Council which underpin other service delivery.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 Service Risk Register - Risks only
findings.headline: Legal services budget risk, scored 12 (probability 4, impact 3), says unexpected corporate issues will drive external legal costs and 'an overspend on the legal services budget'.
findings.detail: The register links the overspend to capacity issues and to the inability to use the usual EM Lawshare Framework procurement route, which means using higher-priced frameworks. The consequence recorded is budgetary pressure. The risk is owned by Emma Griffiths.
findings.matters: A council that cannot use its usual procurement framework and pays higher prices for external legal work will see the overspend in its budget, which is a cost driver other councils can test for.
findings.figures: risk score 12 (probability 4, impact 3)
findings.quote: as unexpected corporate issues arise, external legal costs increase, which will lead to an overspend on the legal services budget

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 Service Risk Register - Risks only
findings.headline: Economy, Regeneration & Sustainability staff budget, scored 16 (probability 4, impact 4), 'relies capitalising time and external funding sources'.
findings.detail: The register says that without this funding, the Council would be unable to maintain staffing levels for city centre management and economic development. Staff would be lost, and the register says these staff have often been difficult to recruit. The risk is owned by Carolyn Ploszynski.
findings.matters: A staffing budget that depends on capitalising staff time and external funding is a structure other councils also use, and its exposure is worth checking against the same assumptions.
findings.figures: risk score 16 (probability 4, impact 4)
findings.quote: Staff budget relies capitalising time and external funding sources

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 Service Risk Register - Risks only
findings.headline: Capital receipts risk, scored 4 (probability 2, impact 2), states that a shortfall causes 'increased borrowing or reduction in capital programme'.
findings.detail: The register attributes the risk to market forces and dependence on third parties. The risk is linked to selling from the investment portfolio, which would reduce income.
findings.matters: A capital receipts shortfall is a common route from asset sales into extra borrowing, so the link is worth comparing with other councils' disposal programmes.
findings.figures: risk score 4 (probability 2, impact 2)
findings.quote: Reduced capital causes increased borrowing or reduction in capital programme

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 Service Risk Register - Risks only
findings.headline: Savings risk, scored 12 (probability 3, impact 4), says savings 'may not be achieved because savings were developed without the input of the service area'.
findings.detail: The consequence is financial impact to the Council and/or service reductions to cut costs, which would affect service quality. The risk is owned by Hagan Lewisman.
findings.matters: It names a specific cause of undelivered savings, namely how they were set, which is a process question for any finance team holding savings targets.
findings.figures: risk score 12 (probability 3, impact 4)
findings.quote: Desired savings may not be achieved because savings were developed without the input of the service area

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 Service Risk Register - Risks only
findings.headline: Outturn forecasting risk (score 6, probability 2, impact 3) records 'significant efficiency savings and service reductions across the board' that may be hard to deliver or to track in time.
findings.detail: The register's stated consequence is increased use of reserve balances or further reductions to be identified. The risk is owned by Clare Paterson.
findings.matters: It shows the link between savings that are difficult to track and a call on reserves, which a finance director at another council can use to test their own savings tracking.
findings.figures: risk score 6 (probability 2, impact 3)
findings.quote: There are significant efficiency savings and service reductions across the board as a result of budget process

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 Service Risk Register - Risks only
findings.headline: Insurance risk (score 8, probability 2, impact 4) records that the Council 'is unable to go to tender' until it improves its property information, and that unoccupied properties over £1m are uninsured.
findings.detail: Only one insurer quoted at the last tender, and the register says the cover has 'significant weaknesses'. The Council's properties are insured on a declared value basis and may be underinsured because of inflation.
findings.matters: A council that cannot go to tender on its insurance and has uninsured properties is carrying risk that a finance director elsewhere would want to know how to price and disclose.
findings.figures: risk score 8 (probability 2, impact 4); unoccupied properties over £1m uninsured
findings.quote: Unoccupied properties over £1m are uninsured. The Council is unable to go to tender before it improves the information that it has.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 Service Risk Register - Risks only
findings.headline: Safety of investments, scored 10 (probability 2, impact 5), records 'Loss of principal investments placed' as the consequence.
findings.detail: The register attributes the risk to prolonged volatility in financial markets, bank and investment institutions not being robust enough to survive future economic changes, and key staffing changes at firms. The risk is owned by Bill Lewis.
findings.matters: It is the Council's own treasury-side risk statement on the security of deposits, which lenders and peer treasury teams read against their counterparty policies.
findings.figures: risk score 10 (probability 2, impact 5)
findings.quote: Loss of principal investments placed

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 Service Risk Register - Risks only
findings.headline: The affordable housing risk scored 20 (probability 4, impact 5) says the Council 'may not be able to access grant to deliver the Council's Affordable Housing Programme'.
findings.detail: The risk is tied to failing to evidence adherence to the Social Housing Regulator's consumer standards. The register notes that a body of compliance work exists, but the full programme is still to be delivered.
findings.matters: Loss of grant would shift the cost of the affordable housing programme onto the Council's own resources, which is a funding question any lender to a housing authority would ask.
findings.figures: risk score 20 (probability 4, impact 5)
findings.quote: The Council may not be able to access grant to deliver the Council's Affordable Housing Programme.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 Service Risk Register - Risks only
findings.headline: Housing delivery risk (score 9, probability 3, impact 3) lists limits to HRA borrowing capacity and 'Borrowing cost rises making schemes unviable' as causes.
findings.detail: The risk also covers changes to the HRA Business Plan and loss of Homes England funding. If grant terms are not met, the register says grant, including RRTBRs, could be returned with punitive interest.
findings.matters: A council whose HRA borrowing headroom and scheme viability depend on borrowing costs is exposed to the same rate sensitivity that other councils are managing.
findings.figures: risk score 9 (probability 3, impact 3); grant returned 'with punitive interest'
findings.quote: Borrowing cost rises making schemes unviable

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 Service Risk Register - Risks only
findings.headline: Housing demand risk, scored 15 (probability 3, impact 5), records overspends 'of a scale that risk the financial stability of the Council'.
findings.detail: The risk covers rising rents, changes to eligibility and homelessness demand, which increase temporary accommodation placements and costs. The register rates the overall impact as a risk that could undermine the Council's ability to perform statutory functions and remain financially stable.
findings.matters: It puts a specific figure on how a demand-led housing cost could reach the general fund, which a finance officer elsewhere can compare with their own temporary accommodation budget.
findings.figures: risk score 15 (probability 3, impact 5)
findings.quote: Risk of overspends of a scale that risk the financial stability of the Council.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 Service Risk Register - Risks only
findings.headline: The HRA risk register scores at 16 (probability 4, impact 4) the risk that HRA income and expenditure cannot be clearly accounted for and evidenced.
findings.detail: The register links missing visibility of HRA income and expenditure to unexpected overspends. It says these would affect the Council's medium term financial plan (MTFP). The risk is owned by Nerys Parry.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council with a ring-fenced HRA will recognise the same exposure: an HRA whose spending is not visible can move the general fund's MTFP.
findings.figures: risk score 16 (probability 4, impact 4)
findings.quote: If there is no clear visibility on expenditure and income of the HRA account there is a potential for unexpected overspends that impact the Council's MTFP.

findings.paper_title: OCC_from reset to recovery_A&GC briefing pack
findings.headline: EY says the PPE matter can be addressed through a full valuation in 2025/26, supported by sufficient evidence.
findings.detail: The paper sets out a remedy for the PPE gap: a full valuation in 2025/26 with sufficient supporting evidence. It is presented as within the council's control.
findings.matters: It states a specific remedy and year for closing a PPE assurance gap, which other councils with similar valuation backlogs can compare against their own plans.
findings.figures: 2025/26 (year of full valuation). No monetary or percentage figures stated for Oxford in the text.
findings.quote: This matter can be addressed by the Council if they perform a full valuation in 2025/26 and can provide sufficient supporting evidence.

findings.headline: EY reports Oxford City Council's audit progress is "slightly behind" the timescales in LARRIG 01, linked to limited 2023/24 audit procedures over PPE valuation support.
findings.detail: The paper says the council's audit progress is behind the LARRIG 01 timescales. It attributes this to limited procedures completed in 2023/24, because the council did not produce adequate support for its PPE valuation procedures.
findings.matters: A PPE valuation evidence gap delays audit sign-off, and EY says assurance gaps can compound into disclaimers in later years, which affects any finance director or lender relying on the audited balance sheet.

findings.detail: The register records this as part of funding from revolving loans and ES reserves for feasibility and focused projects supporting the council's Net Zero targets. The plan for 2025-26 use was recorded, with 2026-27 to be re-confirmed.
findings.matters: A fixed annual reserve contribution is a committed use of funds that a finance director would need to confirm against other calls on the same reserves.

findings.headline: EV charger installation is recorded as 'Behind', with 300 chargers due across Oxford in the next 2 years.
findings.detail: The register says installation is behind because of LEVI programme delays. It also says the rollout needs to continue at pace and be maintained after initial funds.
findings.matters: Delays to externally funded programmes such as LEVI affect the timing of council capital and maintenance commitments, and peers running similar programmes would compare progress.
findings.figures: 300 chargers, next 2 years
findings.quote: Behind. 300 chargers due to be installed across Oxford in the next 2 years.

findings.headline: The decision on the City Centre District Heat Network has been extended from July 2026 to 31 October 2026.
findings.detail: The register says the decision was delayed by a DESNZ review and procurement. The register gives a connection date of 2030 for the phase 1 programme.
findings.matters: A capital decision that has slipped by three months, with its connection date unchanged, is a deadline a finance director elsewhere would want to see tracked.

findings.headline: The Oxford Flood Alleviation Scheme's Compulsory Purchase Order was confirmed in May 2025, with construction due to start late in 2026.
findings.detail: The register says completion will take five years. The scheme provides bunds and a flood plain channel to direct fluvial flood waters away from residential areas.
findings.matters: A multi-year flood scheme is a capital commitment whose timetable and cost a finance director, or a lender to the council, would track through to completion.

findings.headline: Reliance on locums is continuing in 2026-27, with no clear timeline for reducing it.
findings.detail: The register says this creates potential budgetary pressure. It also notes retention difficulties and interim resources being used to clear information governance backlogs.
findings.matters: Agency and locum spend is a recurring cost that a finance director would need to forecast, and it is a cost that peers facing the same recruitment market also carry.
findings.quote: Current reliance on locums is continuing in 26/27, and at present, no clear timelines are possible for reducing this, leading to potential budgetary pressure.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Corporate Risk Register - Risks and Controls
findings.headline: Government changes to the metrics and formula for the Homelessness Prevention Grant are expected later in the year.
findings.detail: The register says the changes could affect the council's future allocation. It links this to rising General Fund pressure from temporary accommodation placements.
findings.matters: Changes to a grant formula alter the income a council can rely on, so peers would want to model their own exposure to the same change.
findings.quote: Government changes to metrics and formula within the Homelessness Prevention Grant are expected later in the year.

findings.headline: Housing Services plans to build temporary accommodation stock from 100 to 350 by December 2026.
findings.detail: The register describes this as a set of measures to manage demand and financial pressure on the council. The control is recorded as in place, with embedding of mitigation actions ongoing.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation placements are a General Fund cost pressure, and a finance director at another council would compare its own TA cost trajectory against this plan.
findings.figures: 100 to 350 temporary accommodation stock by Dec 2026
findings.quote: Housing Services are delivering a wide range of new temporary accommodation measures - to build stock from 100 to 350 by Dec 2026.

findings.headline: The financial MOU has been updated in a Financial Framework document, giving greater clarity on likely LGR cost impacts for the council.
findings.detail: The register records this as a completed update to the MOU. It also notes that the resourcing plan for the systemwide PMO has been put on hold pending the Government's LGR review.
findings.matters: A written financial framework for shared reorganisation costs is what other councils in a joint programme would need to agree before committing budget.
findings.quote: Financial MOU has been updated in a Financial Framework document - providing greater clarity on likely LGR cost impacts for the council.

findings.headline: The register says there may not be full clarity on future LGR costs for the council within the normal Budget/MTFS timeline.
findings.detail: The register attributes this to a review timeframe that will be set by Government. It records that the review of timelines and resourcing against LGR decision scenarios is underway.
findings.matters: Unquantified reorganisation costs that fall outside the budget cycle are a risk a finance director needs to disclose and plan around.
findings.quote: there may not be full clarity on future LGR costs for the council within the normal Budget/MTFS process timeline.

findings.headline: The LGR programme has been paused by Government, and the council reports good progress on funding and financial management arrangements.
findings.detail: The register says the council is positioned to step up progress if and when the programme resumes. The pause is also cited as adding uncertainty to future financial planning.
findings.matters: Local government reorganisation changes the financial base and borrowing position of every council in the area, so a finance director at a peer council would want to see how another handled a pause.
findings.quote: LGR programme has been paused by Government but good progress has been made in terms of both the funding and financial management arrangements

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Corporate Risk Register - Risks and Controls
findings.headline: The budget is described as 'appropriate and deliverable' at this point in 2026-27, in line with the S25 statement.
findings.detail: The register records that the budget was judged appropriate and deliverable when it was set, and that budget management will need to be maintained to deliver a balanced outturn. It also notes that LGR costs may rise in the short term.
findings.matters: A section 25 statement is the chief finance officer's formal view on budget robustness, and finance directors elsewhere track how that view is reaffirmed in-year.
findings.quote: At this point in the financial year, in line with the S25 statement when the budget was set, the budget is considered to be appropriate and deliverable.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Corporate Risk Register - Risks and Controls
findings.headline: Further challenges have been identified in relation to the HRA and returns from OX Place.
findings.detail: The register says the identification of these challenges demonstrated the effectiveness of in-year monitoring. OX Place is one of the council's companies, which the register says must deliver returns through quarterly monitoring.
findings.matters: Company returns to the council are income a finance director has to forecast, and a shortfall would need to be covered from elsewhere.
findings.quote: Further challenges have been identified in relation to the HRA and returns from OX Place, albeit that this has demonstrated the effectiveness of the in-year monitoring.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Corporate Risk Register - Risks and Controls
findings.headline: A budgeting issue identified in the HRA in 2026 has surfaced budget pressures that were already in existence.
findings.detail: The register says these pressures need to be addressed to ensure the sustainability of the HRA over the medium term. The risk is linked to the wider loss of stability from unresolved pressures.
findings.matters: HRA sustainability over the medium term is a core concern for any finance officer managing a housing revenue account and for lenders assessing that income base.
findings.quote: The budgeting issue identified within the HRA in 2026 has surfaced budget pressures that were already in existence

findings.matters: A finance director, here or at another council, would want to know whether a year-end outturn has rebuilt the risk reserve that is meant to absorb pressures.

findings.paper_title: BDO - OCC - 26-27 - Internal Audit Follow Up of Recommendations Report - October 2026
findings.headline: Leisure contracts: management's tracker records two maintenance recommendations as closed, but internal audit says the evidence shows actions agreed rather than changes implemented.
findings.detail: The recommendations require Serco's maintenance tasks to carry risk levels, due dates and completion records, and the Evolution system's priority timing to be corrected. Internal audit says no completed Evolution report or updated client pack has been provided, and it will follow up at the revised date.
findings.matters: A difference between a management tracker marking an action closed and the auditor's view that it is still open is the kind of gap a finance director needs to resolve before relying on contractor reporting.

findings.paper_title: BDO - OCC - 26-27 - Internal Audit Follow Up of Recommendations Report - October 2026
findings.headline: Fire safety follow-up: management has stopped using a supplier pending procurement checks, and the audit has not yet seen the approval, due-diligence or value-for-money evidence.
findings.detail: The recommendation covers new suppliers engaged for health and safety work and whether due process, due diligence and value for money were followed. Management reports that the supplier has not been engaged further, but internal audit says the evidence does not yet confirm the framework or procurement approval.
findings.matters: Procurement of safety-critical suppliers without documented value-for-money and due diligence is a control question other councils would also have to answer.
findings.figures: Original due date 01/07/2026; revised date 31/12/2026
findings.quote: Management has taken action to address the risk identified, including ceasing further use of the supplier while the appropriate framework arrangements are progressed

findings.paper_title: BDO - OCC - 26-27 - Internal Audit Follow Up of Recommendations Report - October 2026
findings.headline: Two QL Optimisation recommendations on purchase order checks and verification of repair works before payment to ODS remain overdue, with a revised completion date of 31/12/2026.
findings.detail: The recommendations cover checking purchase orders before payment to ODS and verifying that repair and maintenance jobs are completed to a satisfactory standard before payment. Management says these are being implemented with the consultants ARK, and the responsible manager has changed.
findings.matters: The gap is between payment and verification of work, so it bears directly on what a council pays its arm's-length contractor for.
findings.figures: Original due dates 30/11/2025 and 30/04/2026; revised date 31/12/2026
findings.quote: Two recommendations relating to purchase order verification and checks over the satisfactory completion of repair and maintenance works remain overdue.

findings.paper_title: BDO - OCC - 26-27 - Internal Audit Follow Up of Recommendations Report - October 2026
findings.headline: The Income Generation recommendation on reconciling rent billed to tenants with the property database has been overdue since 31/03/2025 and now has a revised date of 31/12/2026.
findings.detail: The recommendation asks whether the new asset management system can interface with Agresso to reconcile rent billed against the property management database. Procurement is in progress following Cabinet approval to tender, and implementation is expected after the procurement is complete.
findings.matters: A rent-billing reconciliation that has slipped across four revised dates shows the timing risk of tying a finance control to a system procurement.
findings.quote: The Income Generation recommendation remains overdue.

findings.paper_title: BDO - OCC - 26-27 - Internal Audit Follow Up of Recommendations Report - October 2026
findings.headline: 73% of audit recommendations made since 2023/24 are reported as complete, with 6% in progress, 4% overdue and 18% not yet due.

findings.paper_title: HRA Budget report July 2026 v4
findings.headline: Emerging HRA pressures from waking watch service and housing stock damp and mould issues
findings.detail: Beyond the rental income error, Q1 2026-27 outturn forecast shows emerging budget pressures linked to establishing waking watch service for tower block safety and potential costs from damp and mould in housing stock. Council plans to offset pressures with efficiency savings and longer-term housing improvements.
findings.matters: HRA faces ongoing cost pressures beyond this year's one-off error; these could affect future reserve positions and capital borrowing needs

findings.paper_title: HRA Budget report July 2026 v4
findings.headline: Council implementing enhanced controls to prevent budget model errors recurring
findings.detail: New quality assurance measures include reconciliations between rent calculations and budget, additional oversight processes, and consideration of annual independent review by housing finance expert or internal audit. Audit and Governance Committee will receive an update on these changes.
findings.matters: Shows management's response to control failure and commitment to prevent future income surprises in the HRA
findings.figures: None

These will include but not be limited to, reconciliations between the calculation of rents set with the rental income budget, additional oversight and quality assurance processes to validate the financial model.

findings.paper_title: HRA Budget report July 2026 v4
findings.headline: HRA rental income budget for 2026-27 overestimated by £3.848m due to financial model retaining previous year's CPI rate instead of updating for current year
findings.detail: The financial model used to calculate the HRA's rental income retained the previous year's CPI rate instead of being updated for 2026-27. The budget was approved in February 2026 with this error. While the actual rents charged to tenants were calculated correctly, the budget model overestimated income by £3.848m.
findings.matters: Budget setting errors indicate control weaknesses; lenders assess whether a council can reliably forecast income and manage financial planning
findings.figures: £3.848 million overestimation due to wrong CPI rate
findings.quote: This financial model had not been updated for the relevant CPI rate, instead the rate relevant to the previous financial year was left unchanged.  This meant that the CPI rate applied to calculating the rental income budget was incorrect and the rental income budget was over-estimated.

findings.paper_title: HRA Budget report July 2026 v4
findings.headline: Council must draw down £3.5m HRA reserves due to rental income miscalculation
findings.detail: A technical error left the previous year's CPI rate in the budget model instead of updating it for 2026-27, overestimating rental income by £3.848m. Instead of the forecasted £1.47m surplus, the HRA faces a £2.030m deficit. The council is drawing £3.5m from reserves to balance the budget.
findings.matters: Drawing down reserves reduces the HRA's buffer to absorb future shocks; lenders need to understand the trajectory of reserve positions and their adequacy
findings.figures: £3.5 million reserves drawdown; £3.848 million income overestimation; original budgeted surplus £1.47 million; revised deficit £2.030 million
findings.quote: In order to rectify the issue identified, reserves totalling £3.5 million will need to be drawn down, representing the net movement between the original budgeted surplus of £1.47 million and the revised position that reflects a deficit for the year of £2.030 million.

findings.paper_title: Equality-Impact-Assessment_Community Investments report July 2026
findings.headline: Council is deploying £295,000 from its Risk Reserve to fund one-off community investments.
findings.detail: Oxford is using £115,000 from Community Services Carry Forward Reserve and £295,000 from the Risk Reserve to fund community improvements, democratic transparency initiatives, and youth employment schemes. findings.headline: Service investments (loans to companies for service delivery) forecast to reach £16m in 2026/27 and peak at £30m in 2028/29, with General Fund dependent on 9.1% of revenue from service investment income

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement forecast to grow from £418.3m (2024/25 actual) to £999.3m (2029/30), nearly doubling over the six-year period
findings.detail: The CFR represents the Council's total outstanding capital expenditure not yet paid for from revenue or capital resources. Table 7 shows consistent growth each year, driven by sustained prudential borrowing. The movement in CFR ranges from £89.7m to £159.1m annually, with particularly large increases in 2026/27 and 2029/30.
findings.matters: The CFR is the fundamental measure of a council's debt burden and underlying borrowing need; doubling to nearly £1bn represents a major structural increase in long-term indebtedness that will require sustained revenue contributions to service.
findings.figures: CFR 2024/25 actual £418.3m; 2026/27 forecast £668.9m; 2029/30 forecast £999.3m. Year-on-year movements range from £89.7m to £159.1m
findings.quote: The CFR is simply the total historic outstanding capital expenditure which has not yet been paid for from either revenue or capital resources. It is essentially a measure of the Council's indebtedness and so its underlying borrowing need

findings.headline: HRA net borrowing costs forecast to rise from 16.7% of HRA revenue stream in 2024/25 to 39.6% by 2029/30, with annual borrowing interest climbing from £10.2m to £34.2m
findings.detail: The Council explicitly notes and monitors this trajectory. Paragraph 10 states that a 40-year HRA business plan shows this level of borrowing is affordable, but the council is monitoring it 'on an ongoing basis to ensure that the level of HRA debt does not become unaffordable'. Table 6 shows the financing cost ratio rising from -16.7% to -40.1% over six years.
findings.matters: A doubling of borrowing costs as a proportion of revenue is a material change in HRA affordability; the explicit monitoring language indicates this is being tracked as a risk factor that could constrain future housing investment.

This sharp increase in capital spending requires prudential borrowing of £171.8m compared to £94.1m in 2025/26, an 82% increase in borrowing need.
findings.matters: Large increases in capital spending and associated borrowing represent major financial policy decisions that directly affect a council's debt position and future revenue costs through increased interest payments.
findings.figures: 2026/27 total capital expenditure £233.1m; prudential borrowing £171.8m. 2025/26 forecast £157.8m expenditure; borrowing £94.1m

findings.headline: HRA debt affordability constrained by interest cover ratio of 1.25:1, with £450.2m borrowing planned
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account plans £450.2m borrowing over 2026/27-2029/30 for capital spending. HRA affordability is managed through an agreed interest cover ratio (operating surplus ÷ interest cost) maintained at 1.25:1 minimum, providing limited headroom for rent income variation or cost pressures.
findings.matters: HRA has no Minimum Revenue Provision requirement, so affordability depends entirely on rent income and business plan performance; a 1.25:1 interest cover ratio is tight and leaves no slack for adverse variances.
findings.figures: HRA borrowing 2026/27-2029/30: £450.2m; Interest cover ratio minimum: 1.25:1
findings.quote: The Housing Revenue Account Capital Programme is largely funded from council house rents over time but includes £450.2 million borrowing over the years 2026/27 to 2029/30. findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy 2026 27 v4 (2)
findings.headline: Reserve balances forecast to decline, eliminating internal borrowing capacity and forcing external market reliance
findings.detail: The strategy explicitly forecasts that reserves and balances will reduce over the short to medium term. The council currently has £102.6m of internal borrowing (using reserve funds to self-fund capital), but this capacity will disappear as reserves deplete.

findings.matters: Interest costs are a fixed commitment that reduces budget flexibility; rapid growth signals deteriorating debt serviceability and rising revenue pressure.

Prudential borrowing will rise from £509.8m to £999.3m in the same period.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Budget Review Group Report 2026-27
findings.headline: Union Street car park income projection at high risk; developer assessment outdated and market conditions weakened
findings.detail: The budget assumes £125k per annum income over four years from the Union Street car park site. This remains a higher risk assumption because the site is constrained, delivery option not yet decided, and the income estimate is based on a developer assessment from several years ago. Officers acknowledge that changing market conditions mean the final figure may be lower.
findings.matters: Another income stream flagged by scrutiny as at-risk, compounding already-identified parking revenue volatility from the congestion charge.
findings.figures: £125k per annum projected income over four years
findings.quote: This remains a higher risk assumption as the site is constrained and the preferred delivery option is not yet decided, with both housing and student accommodation still under consideration. The estimated income figure was based on a developer-led assessment from a number of years ago, and while a financial return is still expected, the changing market conditions mean that final figure may be lower.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Budget Review Group Report 2026-27
findings.headline: ICT spending continues to exceed budget assumptions; legacy contracts and licensing driving overruns
findings.detail: ICT expenditure has continued to exceed earlier assumptions. Key drivers include a legacy data-centre contract from 2016 and Microsoft licensing that has increased approximately 20% year-on-year alongside introduction of new products. Forecasting remains difficult given the number of contracts and pace of supplier pricing changes. Cloud migration introduces continuous revenue costs rather than reducing existing costs.
findings.matters: ICT is a non-discretionary service with cost growth that the council cannot easily control or forecast. Ongoing 20% licensing inflation against a fixed budget is a structural pressure.
findings.figures: Microsoft licensing increases approximately 20% year-on-year
findings.quote: Officers explained that a significant driver remains a legacy data-centre contract Council entered into in 2016, with additional pressures arising from Microsoft licensing, which has seen increases of around 20% year-on-year alongside the introduction of new products and application-specific licences.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Budget Review Group Report 2026-27
findings.headline: Real-terms funding cut: zero cash increase in core spending power despite inflation pressures
findings.detail: The government's provisional three-year local government finance settlement results in cash-terms zero increase in core spending power for Oxford in 2026-27, which represents a real-terms reduction once inflation is taken into account. The settlement is driven primarily by assumed council tax rises rather than new government grant funding.
findings.matters: A real-terms cut to core funding creates structural budget pressure that cannot be resolved through efficiency alone, especially given inflation in pay, contracts and construction costs already built into the budget.
findings.figures: Cash-terms zero increase in 2026/27 core spending power
findings.quote: For Oxford City Council, the settlement results in cash-terms zero increase in core spending power in 2026/27, which compares relatively favourably with several neighbouring districts though this still represents real-terms reduction once inflation is taken into account.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Budget Review Group Report 2026-27
findings.headline: £32 million borrowing programme for housing acquisition to stabilise temporary accommodation costs
findings.detail: The budget sets aside £32 million for property acquisition, primarily through the Housing Revenue Account where borrowing is more affordable, as a strategic shift to reduce the council's exposure to rising temporary accommodation market costs.
findings.matters: This is a significant new borrowing commitment driven by inability to control TA costs through other means. It shifts the risk from annual rental volatility to long-term debt servicing.
findings.figures: £32 million
findings.quote: the budget sets aside £32 million, to reflect a strategic shift towards property acquisition, primarily through the Housing Revenue Account where borrowing is more affordable. This should reduce TA costs and limit the Council's exposure to costly TA markets, ultimately stabilising the spend over time.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Budget Review Group Report 2026-27
findings.headline: Garden waste subscribers fell 10% following 10% price increase in 2025/26; scrutiny group questioned whether council has reached tipping point
findings.detail: Garden waste charging was increased 10% in 2025-26 but subscriber numbers fell 10% in the same period. The scrutiny group expressed concern about whether the council has reached a tipping point where further price increases are driving cancellations and undermining overall revenue. Oxford charges among the highest nationally for this service.
findings.matters: Loss of price elasticity is a warning sign. If further increases cause proportionally larger cancellations, revenue deteriorates despite higher charges — a compounding pressure.
findings.figures: 10% reduction in subscribers; 10% price increase in 2025-26
findings.quote: a 10% reduction in the number of garden waste subscribers has occurred alongside a 10% price increase in 2025-26. The Group asked whether the council has reached a tipping point at which further prices increases are driving cancellations thereby undermining overall revenue.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Budget Review Group Report 2026-27
findings.headline: Parking income hit by congestion charge — city centre revenue down £80-100k per month after introduction
findings.detail: Following the recent introduction of a congestion charge, city centre car park ticket purchases have fallen by approximately 25%, while Park & Ride usage increased by 8%. Specific car parks show material declines: Oxpens typically generates £150k per month but fell to £67k in November; Worcester Street normally generates £200k per month but earned £130-150k in November. Officers note forecasting is challenging and updated projections are being developed for the February budget report, with potential draw on reserves if needed.
findings.matters: Parking revenue is budgeted income. A sustained 25% drop in city-centre usage is material and introduces significant forecast uncertainty just as the council is already planning to draw reserves.
findings.figures: Oxpens: £150k per month normal vs £67k November; Worcester Street: £200k per month normal vs £130-150k November; city centre tickets down ~25%; P&R usage up ~8%
findings.quote: Officers pointed out that preliminary figures suggested a significant reduction in income at some city centre car parks. For example, Oxpens typically generates around £150k per month, but income in November fell to approximately £67k. Worcester Street, which normally generate around £200k per month, was currently estimated to have earned between £130k and £150k for November.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Budget Review Group Report 2026-27
findings.headline: Council drawing down up to £8 million in reserves over four-year MTFP to balance budget
findings.detail: The budget plan allows for use of up to £8 million in reserves over the full medium-term financial plan period. This use is described as necessary to keep the budget balanced in the short term but emphasised as unsustainable if continued indefinitely.
findings.matters: Reserve drawdown indicates the council cannot balance recurring expenditure against recurring revenue, creating a structural deficit being masked by one-time resources. Depletion limits the buffer for volatility.
findings.figures: £8 million over MTFP period (2026-27 to 2029-30)
findings.quote: the MTFP allowing for use of up to £8 million over the term. However, while this enabled the budget to remain balanced in the short term, it was strongly emphasised that this would not be a sustainable position if continued indefinitely.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Budget Review Group Report 2026-27
findings.headline: Finance Director retiring — Nigel Kennedy steps down after directing budget preparation
findings.detail: The Group Finance Director, Nigel Kennedy, who leads budget forecasts and financial analysis, is taking retirement after this budget cycle. This is noted as significant timing for the budget process.
findings.matters: A change in the finance leadership during a period of substantial uncertainty (LGR, funding cuts, volatile income streams) introduces transition risk and potential loss of institutional knowledge during a complex operational period.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: This year's Budget preparations are particularly poignant since they are the last ones that Nigel Kennedy will direct before he takes a well-earned retirement.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Budget Review Group Report 2026-27
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation costs already overrunning budget in year three, despite annual projections
findings.detail: By Q3 of the current year, spending on temporary accommodation was already approaching the full-year budget of £2.6 million, and officers acknowledged that on current trends a gross overspend is likely. The scrutiny group noted that historically budgets have underestimated this pressure. TA costs are heavily influenced by external factors like the economy and government policy, with small changes producing movements of hundreds of thousands of pounds.
findings.matters: TA is a volatile, growing liability that the council has repeatedly underbudgeted. Unchecked cost growth here is a structural pressure on the council's financial position.
findings.figures: £2.6 million full-year budget; approximately £500k rental income collected by mid-year suggesting ~£1m annually; £32 million allocated for property acquisition as mitigation
findings.quote: by the third quarter, spend was already approaching the full-year budget of £2.6 million. Officers acknowledged that, on current trends, a gross overspend is likely, though this may be partially mitigated by rental income and new TA stock coming on stream in the final quarter.

findings.paper_title: Oxford Capital Strategy 2026-27 V1
findings.headline: The council plans £489.43 million of new prudential borrowing over four years (£39.25 million General Fund, £450.18 million HRA), substantially increasing the debt burden.
findings.detail: This borrowing is to fund housing company loans, social housing, and operational capital schemes. The strategy notes this assumes 'full funding of the capital programme without the application of an optimism bias', meaning it is a baseline case, not a downside scenario. New borrowing brings Minimum Revenue Provision charges to the revenue account (except for loans to companies assumed to be repaid).
findings.matters: A lender needs to verify that new borrowing is affordable within the council's revenue budget and that the MRP charges do not destabilise reserves or force service cuts. The scale is material relative to a council the size of Oxford.
findings.figures: £489.43 million net prudential borrowing 2026/27–2029/30; £39.25 million General Fund, £450.18 million HRA.
findings.quote: There is approximately £489.43 million of net Prudential Borrowing anticipated from 2026/27 up to and including 2029/30. Of this, £39.25 million relates to General Fund financing and £450.18 million relates to HRA financing.

findings.paper_title: Oxford Capital Strategy 2026-27 V1
findings.headline: Council's £145.8m property portfolio facing tenant stress; monitoring shifted to shorter-term focus due to energy and inflation pressures
findings.detail: The council owns investment property with a gross book value of £145.8 million generating £11.02 million in annual rent (2024/25). The council reports that 'the focus has shifted to a shorter view because of the general economic pressures as a result of energy and inflation', and has implemented a tracker to monitor tenant arrears. This signals active tenant distress, not routine management.
findings.matters: A large property portfolio under tenant stress from energy/inflation is a leading indicator of rental decline and impairment risk. For a lender, it signals whether this income stream can be relied on to service debt or support capital projects.
findings.figures: Gross book value £145.8 million; rent receivable 2024/25 £11.02 million.
findings.quote: The focus has shifted to a shorter view because of the general economic pressures as a result of energy and inflation. A tracker has been implemented which considers current arrears positions and records a summary of the latest position and contacts with tenants.

findings.paper_title: Oxford Capital Strategy 2026-27 V1
findings.headline: The council acknowledges significant financial pressures in coming years and is shelving zero-carbon requirements in capital projects because they have become unaffordable.
findings.detail: The strategy states that inflationary pressures are making green building standards uneconomic for projects that do not generate income, and explicitly links this to 'significant financial pressures faced by the council in the coming years'. This is not routine cost pressure; it is forcing a retreat from stated policy due to affordability.
findings.matters: A council that cannot afford green commitments on capital projects is under real revenue stress. This signals tightening budgets and forced prioritisation, which affects both current spending and future service viability.
findings.figures: Projects costed assuming zero-carbon compliance but being built without it where 'budget is available'.
findings.quote: This is accentuated for projects that do not generate income. This is especially relevant given the significant financial pressures faced by the council in the coming years.

findings.paper_title: Oxford Capital Strategy 2026-27 V1
findings.headline: Usable capital receipts fell to £16.4 million from £40.9 million as at 31 March 2025, with limited property available for sale
findings.detail: As of 31 March 2025, the council held £40.9 million in usable capital receipts but after financing capital spend, only £16.4 million remained. The council explicitly states it 'relied heavily' on capital receipts in the past but they are 'gradually being eroded' due to 'limited property available for sale'. This narrows the council's room to flex capital funding when pressures emerge.
findings.matters: Declining receipts reduce a council's ability to fund discretionary capital or respond to urgent need without borrowing. For a lender, it signals tightening financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £40.9 million in usable capital receipts as at 31 March 2025; £16.4 million available after financing.
findings.quote: In the past the Council has relied heavily on capital receipts to fund its General Fund Programme but with limited property available for sale these are gradually being eroded.

findings.paper_title: Oxford Capital Strategy 2026-27 V1
findings.headline: Oxford City Council will cease to exist on 1 April 2028 as part of local government reorganisation, cutting the four-year capital strategy in half.
findings.detail: The council explicitly states that from April 2028, it will cease to exist and its capital expenditure will become the responsibility of a successor authority. This is not a contingency—the strategy is written assuming this happens. For a lender, this means capital commitments made now run into an entity transition midway through the strategy period, raising questions about succession, debt responsibility, and project continuity.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether commitments survive the handover, who assumes the debt, and whether the successor authority has been defined or legally committed. This is not routine risk; it is fundamental structural change.
findings.figures: Four-year strategy to 2029/30; reorganisation date 1 April 2028.
findings.quote: if Local Government Reorganisation continues as expected, from 1st April 2028 Oxford City Council will cease to exist and the capital expenditure from that point onwards will be the responsibility of the successor

findings.paper_title: February Budget Report (4) COUNCIL REPORT (10)
findings.headline: OCHL housing company dividend forecast to stop after 2026-27, with only £3m payable in that year and zero thereafter
findings.detail: The company dividend that was built into the MTFS is now forecast at only £3m for 2026-27 and then nothing. Shareholders were advised in December 2025 that future surpluses are dependent on planning permission for major schemes (Redbridge and Sandy Lane) which is not yet obtained.
findings.matters: A forecast revenue stream the budget depends on is evaporating. Future returns are now contingent on planning approvals that may not materialise.
